overall_summary: Space anomalies and mind-bending physical comparisons drive the highest engagement and views, whereas internal psychological facts and brain-related topics consistently struggle to capture immediate viewer interest.

winning_patterns.evidence: 'The Largest Ocean in Space' (460 views), 'What Does Outer Space Actually Smell Like?' (368 views), and 'The Planet of Burning Ice' (270 views) are the channel's top performers.
winning_patterns.action: Double down on space concepts that contrast extreme physical properties (e.g., fire, ice, smells, oceans) to trigger high curiosity.

winning_patterns.evidence: 'Sharks Are Older Than Trees?' generated 302 views by challenging intuitive timelines.
winning_patterns.action: Create content comparing the age of modern things to ancient prehistoric survivors to disrupt the viewer's sense of time.

weak_patterns.pattern: Abstract Cognitive Psychology and Brain Facts
weak_patterns.evidence: 'Your Brain Can Create Fake Memories' (5-54 views) and 'The Real Reason Songs Get Stuck In Your Head' (17 views) failed to gain traction.
weak_patterns.action: Pivot away from abstract cognitive psychology and focus on tangible, external physical mysteries.

next_video.concept: A planet where the atmosphere is so extreme that it rains molten iron instead of water.
next_video.opening_direction: Show a hyper-realistic animation of a dark storm, asking: 'What if a single raindrop could melt right through your skull?'
next_video.twist_direction: Reveal that on planet WASP-76b, it literally rains liquid iron, and the winds blow this metallic rain sideways at 10,000 miles per hour.
next_video.reason: Leverages the highly successful space category, uses a sensory/physical paradox hook similar to 'burning ice' and 'glass sideways', and targets the peak historic upload window.

experiment: Test a 15-second Short comparing the age of a common cosmic feature (like Saturn's rings) to something unexpected on Earth (like sharks or trees) to replicate the 'Sharks vs. Trees' success.
